analysis.title: The Top-Down Credit Edge: When AI cannibalises hyperscalers
key_insights: Santander's credit desk argues AI capex is outrunning revenue. Steep token price falls and an AI spending peak since August fed the concern, and Anthropic's pre-IPO S1 did not dispel revenue slowdown worries.
3Q earnings added a new angle: AI may cannibalise hyperscalers' core advertising business, the cash engine funding the AI build-out.
Alphabet's Google core advertising revenue growth slowed from +20% y/y to +12% ($63.3bn) in 3Q.

Amazon's advertising revenue grew +11% y/y (about $20bn), below expectations and its lowest growth rate since it began reporting the figure in 2020. Amazon denies a link to AI agents but has blocked Muse (and OpenAI's Dots).

AI agents buying and deciding on behalf of users threaten advertising economics and can disintermediate the customer relationship itself. Muse hit US financials first, where customer inertia behind low-cost deposits came under review.
Alphabet fell 13% (about $500bn) the day before publication, the second-largest one-day market cap loss in Wall Street history behind NVIDIA's roughly 17% ($593bn) drop on 27 Jan 2025 (DeepSeek).
Intel is down about 30% on the day and about 50% from its June peak. SoftBank, an OpenAI investor, is down about 50% since its June peak.
Credit spreads widened sharply before 3Q earnings, already raising return-on-investment questions on AI spending. Credit market signals are starting to reach hyperscalers.

Meta surprised the market by raising equity. Oracle's investor day was bond-friendly: positive FCF targeted in 2H28, debt down to 3.5x EBITDA in 2029, gross debt issuance capped at $10bn next year plus another $10bn of equity. This follows a $25bn bond offering in 2025 and a $20bn equity raise earlier this year.

Microsoft's jumbo bond drew a $115bn book with a bid-to-cover peaking at 4x and final demand about 2.5-3x. It was Microsoft's first US IG deal since 2017 ($17bn). Microsoft and J&J are the only Aaa/AAA US corporates, one notch above S&P's US sovereign rating. Pricing tightened aggressively and attrition was significant.
Credit flows improved this week. EUR IG funds had a fourth straight week of outflows (-$178mn vs -$929mn last week), with the 1-4Y bucket at -$193mn (October -$1.5bn). EUR HY funds took in $506mn.

US credit funds saw $4.6bn of inflows ($2.8bn IG, $1.8bn HY), the largest since early July, with returns of +0.7% IG and +0.8% HY. European equity funds saw -$930mn (third week of outflows) against +$12bn into US equities (third week of inflows).

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers will find new ways to monetize AI traffic, and lower token prices should carry the technology deeper into personal and working life. Strong credits like Microsoft still draw large demand ($115bn book).
tension_points.bear_case: Capex keeps rising while revenue growth fades. AI may cannibalise core advertising (Google ads +12% from +20%, Amazon ads +11%) and agents can disintermediate customer relationships.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further core advertising deceleration at hyperscalers and wider credit spreads would confirm the bear case, while Oracle-style funding discipline would ease credit concerns.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI can not only hurt software companies but can also cannibalise hyperscalers' core advertising business, the cash engine funding the AI build-out.
theme_stances.evidence: AI can not only hurt software companies but it can also cannibalise hyperscalers’ core advertising business

theme_stances.key_argument: Bond and CDS signals are starting to push hyperscalers to change funding, as seen in Meta's equity raise and Oracle's bond-friendly plan.
theme_stances.evidence: Credit investors: the only adults in the room.
